records.name: Monaco
records.summary:
Monaco is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Hate crimes and hate speech based on sexual orientation are penalised, and discrimination on grounds including gender identity is banned. A visitor faces no legal exposure whatsoever: no bathroom laws, no border friction (a tiny tourist enclave embedded in the neighbouring country of France, entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans incidents, and street violence of any kind is rare in this heavily-policed, very low-crime destination.

The score reflects the gap between de facto safety (very high) and legal thinness: no functioning legal gender recognition process and limited explicit trans protections.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (last updated 12 March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections — hate crimes and hate speech on sexual orientation are penalised, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned (reported discrimination is described as rare); same-sex couples have no marriage or adoption, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is limited.

French gay travel guide Monaco page: no gay Pride is held anywhere in Monaco (visitors are sent to France or Italy for one); the ~200-hectare state is pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Nice-Matin via Monaco Haut Commissariat (March 2025, French): homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly 10 people dare to be openly out; Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo: "C’est le triste bilan de Monaco".

Queer In The World Monaco guide (updated 3 December 2023): homosexuality legal and SOGI discrimination illegal only in certain contexts — limited protections with room for improvement; advises visitors to stay current with local laws and customs.

records.name: San Marino
records.summary:
San Marino is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. There is no functioning legal-gender-recognition process (a resident-facing gap only), no criminalisation, no bathroom law, no border friction (open border with the neighbouring country of Italy), and no documented pattern of anti-trans violence in this tiny, heavily tourism-dependent nation surrounded by Italy.

The score reflects very high de facto safety combined with minimal explicit legal infrastructure for trans people. For a visitor, no legal exposure is documented.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map, Legal gender recognition category (2026 edition): San Marino is listed among the countries where there is NO functioning legal or administrative process for legal gender recognition.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 - Legal Gender Recognition chapter: country-by-country findings for 2025, including Albania's rejection of a self-ID recommendation at UPR, trans activist Luana Myrto's legal action in Albania, Andorra's delayed hormone-treatment decree, and other European developments.

ILGA compilation of SOGIESC recommendations from the 34th UPR Working Group session (Nov 2019) - includes San Marino's review among 12 countries examined; documents the SOGIESC recommendations each state received and accepted.
Euronews (4 Jun 2019): citizens voted by referendum to insert a clause prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation into the constitution of San Marino — the motion passed.

The Guardian (4 Apr 2022): Paolo Rondelli appointed captain regent — the world's first openly gay head of state (six-month term, no executive power); the article notes homosexuality was punishable by jail time in San Marino until 2004 and legal recognition of gay couples followed in 2016.
Euronews Italia (16 Nov 2018): San Marino's legislature approved a civil-unions law, described as 'leaner than the Cirinnà' Italian statute — the relationship-recognition framework in force.

records.name: Liechtenstein
records.summary:
Liechtenstein is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Same-sex relations are legal and discrimination based on sexual orientation is banned, but gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are not included in any anti-discrimination legislation, and there is no legal gender recognition law; these gaps are resident-facing, and a visitor faces no legal exposure.

No documented pattern of anti-trans violence, no bathroom law, no border friction (entry under the common border-free travel zone via its neighbours Switzerland and Austria), in a very small, very low-crime country closely integrated with those neighbours. Social attitudes are conservative but not mobilised-hostile. Marriage and joint adoption have been available since January 2025.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): mixed situation - same-sex relations legal and sexual-orientation discrimination banned, but gender identity/expression/sex characteristics not covered by any anti-discrimination law; no legal gender marker change; IGM not prohibited; marriage and joint adoption available since January 2025; the state religion is Roman Catholicism and the archbishop publicly opposed marriage equality; first Pride in 2022.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters feature covers tiny European states (including Liechtenstein) playing catch-up on LGBT equality.

GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Liechtenstein' (March 2012): with a population of ~35,000 there is no organised gay scene - friendship networks are the scene; 'few organized enemies... no religious extremists, no right-wing skinheads, no political rogues demanding homophobic laws'; gay people live comfortably with little interference.

360° magazine (Jan 2016, in French): Prince Hans-Adam II called rainbow families 'irresponsible' in his New Year interview, said children have 'a right to a normal family', and suggested Liechtenstein could 'ignore' an adverse European Court of Human Rights ruling; local LGBT organisation Flay said it was 'choqué'; the Freie Liste called the remarks contrary to the Constitution and the ECHR.

Landtag motion (Sept 2022, in German): 'Motion zur Öffnung der Ehe für alle' - MPs' motion to open civil marriage regardless of gender and sexual orientation, removing all remaining legal differences; notes registered partnerships are seen as a 'second-class marriage' and that the Prince had said in 2021 he had nothing against marriage equality except adoption.

records.name: Vatican City
records.summary:
Vatican City is workable for trans visitors — an unusual case: a tiny 0.49 km² tourist enclave with essentially no resident jurisdiction a traveler can fall afoul of. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; there are no bathroom inspections, no morality police, and the guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of tourists of every presentation visit annually without incident; entry is via the neighbouring city of Rome with no border formality.

The doctrinal climate is hostile — the 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity, and no legal recognition or protection of any kind exists — but this is a climate signal, not a traveler-facing mechanism: the realistic worst case for a visitor is being refused entry to the basilica over a dress-code dispute (shoulders/knees rules apply to everyone).

sources.summary: PinkNews (2 Oct 2008): Catholic officials rejected France's first-choice candidate as ambassador to the Holy See because he is gay, forcing Paris to name a different envoy -- documented instance of the Vatican government refusing an LGBT person in diplomatic relations.

Vatican Congregation for Catholic Education (2019): 'Male and Female He Created Them - Towards a Path of Dialogue on the Question of Gender Theory in Education' - the Vatican's educational document opposing 'gender theory', which it says 'denies the difference and reciprocity in nature of a man and a woman' and 'eliminat[es] the anthropological basis of the family'.

Overview of Fiducia Supplicans: DDF declaration under Pope Francis (issued 20 Mar 2023) permitting spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage; a January 2024 DDF press release reiterated that blessings never extend to the unions themselves -- the current Holy See posture on blessing gay couples (fetched, document coverage verified).

Overview: no documented modern criminal-law persecution of consensual homosexual conduct in Vatican City itself (decriminalisation has nineteenth-century roots); the Holy See's institutional posture against homosexuality and gender theory drives policy -- legal baseline distinguishing the Church's diplomacy from the city-state's own law (fetched, article text verified).

records.name: Cambodia
records.summary:
Cambodia is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — the country has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression — and the government is formally cooperative: it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 Universal Periodic Review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted the UN Independent Expert on SOGI in 2023. Phnom Penh and Siem Reap, the country's two main cities, have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors.

The risks are street-level and police-level rather than legal: a human-rights organisation documents "shocking" harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse). There is no legal gender recognition yet, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute.

For a visitor: low probability of legal trouble; moderate probability of harassment if visibly trans outside tourist areas; police are a risk factor, not a protection, for trans women especially.

sources.summary: UN in Cambodia page for the UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity visit report: identifies good practices and remaining challenges and formulates recommendations to strengthen protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; an unofficial Khmer translation was prepared for national stakeholders.

OutRight International Cambodia profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex sexual activity (French protectorate 1867, independence 1953); at UPR 2019 accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage and at UPR 2024 accepted all 12 LGBTIQ recommendations incl. seven on marriage equality; legislation contains no SOGI non-discrimination provisions.

Phnom Penh Post on a Cambodian Centre for Human Rights (CCHR) report: an overwhelming majority of transgender women on Cambodia's city streets face 'shocking' harassment and abuse (135+ cases documented), including a disturbing Siem Reap police practice of targeting transgender sex workers and forcing them to bathe in dirty, stagnant river water.

Rainbow Community Kampuchea (RoCK) page on Cambodia's 4th-cycle UPR: Cambodia officially accepted all 12 SOGIESC/LGBT+ recommendations in 2024 - marriage equality progress, legal gender recognition for self-defined identity, and anti-discrimination measures; includes the civil-society joint submission (Dec 2023) and summary factsheets.

UNDP/USAID 'Being LGBT in Asia: Cambodia Country Report' (2014): participatory review of the legal and social environment for LGBT persons and civil society, based on the Cambodia National LGBT Community Dialogue (Phnom Penh, Jan 2013), participant conversations, an NGO/CBO survey and a desk review of published literature.
Frommer's travel guide: 'Tips for Gay and Lesbian Travelers' in Cambodia - practical travel advice for LGBT visitors (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

PinkNews (20 Jul 2019) on Rainbow Community Kampuchea (RoCK) study: 81% of queer women and transgender people under 35 suffered emotional abuse by a family member; 35% of under-35 participants considered suicide because of family rejection — including a 27-year-old trans man forced by his mother into rehab to 'fix his gender'.

records.name: Nepal
records.summary:
Nepal is workable for trans visitors — South Asia's most legally recognising country. The Supreme Court has protected gender identity since a landmark 2007 ruling; a third-gender category exists on documents by self-identification; and in 2024 the Supreme Court ruled that a trans woman must be recognised as female without medical verification. Nothing is criminalised, and Kathmandu, the capital, has an established activist scene.

The gap between doctrine and practice is large: an international observer, Human Rights Watch, documents that implementation is piecemeal and humiliating, and trans people in provinces face physical and sexual harassment in public spaces with little police protection. These burdens fall overwhelmingly on residents navigating citizenship documents — a visitor with a foreign passport faces none of the bureaucratic gauntlet.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, tolerant tourist areas, but expect stares and possible harassment if visibly trans outside the main tourist bubbles.

sources.summary: HRW (Feb 2024): calls on Nepal's government to urgently create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure so transgender and third-gender people can obtain official documents — illustrating that despite progressive rulings, no straightforward document-change process exists (photo shows a Kathmandu trans woman holding her 2023 citizenship certificate listing female gender). For this record: official-observer statement on the documentary-recognition gap.

JURIST (Aug 2024): Nepal's Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed 50+ lawsuits since 2021; changing markers to 'female'/'male' has usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations including intrusive post-operative genital exams. For this record: the landmark ruling and the pre-ruling barrier path, dated.

The Diplomat (Feb 2024): Nepal's 2007 ruling allowing self-identified legal gender was novel at the time and later cases reinforced it, but government officials limited changes to people identifying as 'third gender' while male/female marker changes lagged — the country's progressive reputation outruns policy. For this record: documented doctrine-versus-implementation gap.

Kathmandu Post feature (Nov 2024) on trans life in Janakpur: trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are often subjected to physical and sexual harassment. For this record: ground-level conditions for visibly trans people in provincial cities, dated 2024.

APTN (Asia Pacific Transgender Network) publication (Oct 2021, in Nepali): 'Gender Identity Draft Bill 2078: Civil Society Proposal' - by Rukshana Kapali and Allan Bhandari with advocate Subin Mulmi, produced through the Amplifying Trans Advocacy Fellowship; a civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition in Nepal.

The Record (Sept 25, 2020) by Queer Youth Group and Queer Rights Collective: argues that despite the Constitution awarding the right to self-determine name and gender markers (2007 case), 'an extensive overhaul of the law and the language of the law' is still needed to address inequalities faced by the trans and broader PoMSOGIESC community. For this record: local-activist assessment of the gap between constitutional right and statute.

SIT Study Abroad ISP (Spring 2015) by Sophia Greene: 'Gender and Sexuality in Nepal: The Experiences of Sexual and Gender Minorities in a Rapidly Changing Social Climate' - despite changing legislation, sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in virtually every arena of life amid the clash of patriarchal tradition and modernisation.
